title: The Weight Upstairs
passage:
The visitors' gallery on the eighty-first floor of the Verrand Tower sells more tickets than the observation deck above it, and the reason is a ball of laid steel plate the width of a bus, hung on eight cables in a well cut through the building. It is a tuned mass damper. When the wind comes hard off the estuary the ball swings — late, heavily, half a beat behind the tower — and takes the sway out of the floors around it. Visitors photograph it; brochures give it a number. At commissioning, the Verrand's damper cut peak acceleration at the top of the building by two fifths. That figure is honest, and it is the figure the whole argument about tall buildings and wind has been conducted in for thirty years. It describes one afternoon.

Hedda Rask has been collecting the afternoons since. For twelve years her group has kept accelerometers running near the top of nineteen towers in Brayle, sampling continuously rather than in the week of handover tests, and matching the record against the complaint logs floor by floor. On the commissioning figure the dampers did what was claimed of them. In eighteen of the nineteen towers the reduction measured in the first year sat within a percentage point or two of what the designers had predicted, and in the buildings where trouble had been expected — the slender ones, on exposed corners — the complaints did not arrive. Rask says this part of the record is not in dispute. The dampers work, and they work about as well as the brochures say.

What the twelve-year record shows is what happens next. A tuned mass damper is tuned: its mass and its cable length are set against the tower's own natural frequency, and it does its work only in a narrow band around that frequency. Buildings do not stay put. Fit-out adds partitions, tenants add paper and machinery, mechanical rooms take on water, and every addition of mass drags the frequency down. Across the nineteen towers the frequency measured in year ten sat on average some four percent below the value the damper had been set against, and in the three most heavily fitted-out buildings nearer seven. The benefit fell with it. By year eight the median tower was getting rather less than half the reduction it had been commissioned with — not because anything had broken, but because the building had walked away from its own damper. Where a damper was retuned the benefit came back almost in full. Four of the nineteen were retuned.

Towers that manage the wind by their shape do not drift. A profile that tapers, corners that are chamfered or notched, a slot cut through the upper floors: these break up the regular vortex shedding that drives crosswind sway, and they go on breaking it up for as long as the building stands, unattended and unbilled. Constantin Marek, who designed the notched profile of the Ossian, puts it without qualification. "A damper is a maintenance contract you have signed on behalf of everyone who owns the building after you," he says. "A shape is a decision made once. One of those survives a change of owner. The other does not." Rask allows him the first half. "A shape is tuned too," she says. "Not to a frequency — to a wind." The modeling assumes the directions the wind arrives from and the ground it crosses on the way in; when a forty-floor block went up two hundred meters upwind of the Halberd, the accelerometers there recorded a rise in crosswind response that has not gone away. Nobody can notch the Halberd now.

So the damper's advantage decays and can be restored; the shape's advantage does not decay and cannot be. Neither is obviously the safer bet, which may be why the choice so often gets made on the commissioning figure instead: it is available early, it fits in a brochure, and it says nothing about year ten. Rask will not tell an owner which to build. An honest comparison, she thinks, would have to name a maintenance regime alongside the percentage, and the blocks not yet built alongside that — and nobody can do the second. Wind engineering is sold as a problem solved at the ribbon-cutting. It is a problem that has to be kept solved, by somebody, for as long as the tower stands and the skyline around it goes on moving.
— Marcus Ilbery

tuned mass damper = a heavy weight hung inside a tower so that its swing works against the building's own
vortex shedding = the regular peeling-away of air on alternate sides of a tall structure, which pushes it sideways

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: That the tourists filing into the Verrand's gallery are being shown a machine that has quietly stopped earning its keep.
That the two ways of steadying a tower differ less in what they deliver at handover than in what becomes of it later.
That shaping a tower is the better technique, since its benefit, unlike a damper's, never has to be paid for again.
That wind loads on the tallest buildings have been underestimated, and that the margins designers work to should be revised.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text gist), edge position 1. WHY-KEY (B): the arc runs phenomenon → evidence → complication → verdict, and both halves of B are load-bearing. The received figure is the commissioning number ('it is the figure the whole argument about tall buildings and wind has been conducted in for thirty years. It describes one afternoon'); the evidence paragraph confirms the dampers on that figure ('In eighteen of the nineteen towers the reduction measured in the first year sat within a point or two of what the designers had predicted'); the complication is what happens after handover to each technique — the damper drifts out of tune ('By year eight the median tower was getting rather less than half the reduction it had been commissioned with') while the shape holds but can be spoiled by a later neighbor ('the accelerometers there recorded a rise in crosswind response that has not gone away'); and the verdict names the asymmetry outright ('the damper's advantage decays and can be restored; the shape's advantage does not decay and cannot be'). WHY-NOT-A (trap: scope_error / detail-as-main, distorted): the gallery and the photographed sphere open the passage and are vivid, but the text never says the Verrand's damper in particular has lost its effect, and never accuses anyone of misleading visitors — the drift figures are group statistics across nineteen towers, and the complaint is about the metric, not about honesty. A blind reader who fixes on the opening scene finds this live; it promotes a scene-setting detail and misstates the charge. WHY-NOT-C (trap: quantifier_upgrade of a half-truth): the passage does say shaped towers 'do not drift' and work 'unattended and unbilled', so the first clause is real; 'never has to be paid for again' upgrades that into the very claim Rask dismantles, since the Halberd lost response margin to a block built upwind and 'nobody can notch the Halberd now'. It is also Marek's position rather than the text's. WHY-NOT-D (trap: outside_knowledge): structural safety margins under wind load are the most familiar public version of this subject, so a passage-blind reader will consider it, but this text is about occupant sway, accelerometers and complaint logs, and never discusses loads on the frame or design margins at all.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the first year of Rask's accelerometer record?

options.text: In all but one of the nineteen towers the measured reduction landed within a point or two of the designers' prediction.
Most of the towers gained something from their dampers, though the slender ones on the exposed corners gained little.
Even in that first year the reduction achieved bore very little relation to the frequency each damper had been matched to.
Rask's group put each damper through a week of forced-vibration trials before it would certify the commissioning figures.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 2. WHY-KEY (A): 'In eighteen of the nineteen towers the reduction measured in the first year sat within a percentage point or two of what the designers had predicted.' A recasts eighteen-of-nineteen as 'all but one' and 'sat within' as 'landed within' — a paraphrase, not a lift. Note the deliberate hedge inversion demanded by law 10: here the key is the confident, near-absolute claim and the cautious-sounding option is the wrong one, so 'pick the qualified answer' does not work across this unit. WHY-NOT-B (trap: quantifier_downgrade with a scope flaw): it sounds properly measured, and 'slender ones, on exposed corners' is lifted straight from the reader's memory of the paragraph — but the passage says the opposite about exactly those buildings: 'in the buildings where trouble had been expected — the slender ones, on exposed corners — the complaints did not arrive.' WHY-NOT-C (trap: wrong_location, shifted in time): the failure of the frequency setting is paragraph 3's finding about years eight to ten; relocating it to the first year contradicts the first-year result, which matched prediction closely. A skimmer who has read to the end and remembers frequency as the villain accepts it. WHY-NOT-D (trap: outside_knowledge): forced-vibration testing is a real and sensible way to certify a damper, so it reads as competent method, but the text says Rask's group did the reverse — 'sampling continuously rather than in the week of handover tests' — and never mentions any testing they carried out themselves.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the natural frequencies of the towers over the twelve years?

options.text: They rose as fit-out stiffened the structures, which left every damper tuned below the frequency its tower had reached.
They held at the values the designers had chosen, and the lost benefit came instead from wear in the cables and bearings.
Each of the nineteen towers had drifted a full seven percent below its commissioned setting by the tenth year of the record.
They fell as the buildings took on partitions and equipment, moving away from the settings the dampers had been given.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (D): 'Fit-out adds partitions, tenants add paper and machinery, mechanical rooms take on water, and every addition of mass drags the frequency down. Across the nineteen towers the frequency measured in year ten sat on average some four percent below the value the damper had been set against.' D paraphrases both the direction of the change and its cause without reusing the sentence. WHY-NOT-A (trap: reversed detail): stiffening a structure does raise its natural frequency, so this is the physically literate wrong answer, and it recycles the passage's own fit-out material with the arrow inverted; the text attributes the change to added mass and says the frequency is dragged down, not up. WHY-NOT-B (trap: outside_knowledge / plausible mechanism never stated): mechanical wear in cables and bearings is what a reader expects to degrade a moving machine over twelve years, and it would explain the halved benefit — but the passage forecloses it explicitly: the reduction fell 'not because anything had broken, but because the building had walked away from its own damper.' WHY-NOT-C (trap: quantifier_upgrade): the seven percent figure is real but belongs to a named subset — 'in the three most heavily fitted-out buildings nearer seven' — against an average of about four percent. C promotes the extreme of the distribution to a universal, and 'a full seven percent' hardens 'nearer seven' as well.

questions.prompt: Rask says that a shape is tuned as well, though not to a frequency. What does the text suggest follows from this?

options.text: The modeling behind a shaped tower must assume a set of wind directions, and the Halberd's designers chose the wrong ones.
Shaping and damping alike need periodic retuning, and it is really only the cost of that work that separates them.
What a shaped tower is worth against the wind is settled partly by buildings its designers never had the chance to see.
Shaped towers should only be built where zoning can be relied on to keep the blocks around them low.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. The passage lays the two pieces side by side without joining them: the modeling 'assumes the directions the wind arrives from and the ground it crosses on the way in', and 'when a forty-floor block went up two hundred meters upwind of the Halberd, the accelerometers there recorded a rise in crosswind response that has not gone away'. WHY-KEY (C): if the shape's performance is calculated against an assumed approach flow, and a later building alters that approach, then part of what the shape is worth was never in the designer's hands — it is decided by structures that did not exist when the tower was drawn. That join is the single inch the text leaves the reader to walk; it is supported again, obliquely, by the verdict's demand that an honest comparison name 'the blocks not yet built'. WHY-NOT-A (trap: too_literal plus wrong attribution): its first clause restates the premise the stem is built on, so a reader who stops at retrieval feels on firm ground, and it reaches for the passage's most vivid case. Its second clause is the flaw: the passage attributes the Halberd's rise in crosswind response to a forty-floor block that 'went up two hundred meters upwind' after the fact, not to any error in the directions its designers assumed — and it never grades that modeling at all. WHY-NOT-B (trap: surface_word_match on 'tuned', and contradicted): Rask's own word 'tuned' makes this feel like the intended reading, but the passage insists on the asymmetry — a damper can be retuned and the benefit 'came back almost in full', whereas 'Nobody can notch the Halberd now'. Cost is not what separates them; recoverability is. WHY-NOT-D (trap: too_far): a two-step leap into land-use policy. The text describes what an upwind block did to one tower and says nobody can price the blocks not yet built; it recommends nothing about where shaped towers should be permitted, and Rask explicitly 'will not tell an owner which to build'.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to Marek's case against machinery?

options.text: He grants Marek that a shape outlasts its owners, while denying that this is what makes it the safer choice.
He treats the Brayle record as broadly bearing Marek out, with the Halberd standing as a minor exception to it.
He shares Marek's view that a decision taken once is worth more than any arrangement somebody has to keep maintaining.
He finds Marek's preference for shaping a designer's vanity that the accelerometer record has entirely discredited.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / attitude), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (A): the writer concedes Marek's first premise in the text's own voice — 'Towers that manage the wind by their shape do not drift', they work 'unattended and unbilled', and 'Rask allows him the first half' — and then withholds the conclusion Marek draws from it, closing on 'the shape's advantage does not decay and cannot be [restored]. Neither is obviously the safer bet.' Concession plus refusal of the inference is exactly A. WHY-NOT-B (trap: direction reversal, hedged in form): built to sound as measured as the key so that a test-wise 'pick the cautious option' decides nothing. It fails on direction and on scale: the Halberd is not treated as a minor exception but as the case that shows what a shape cannot do, and the passage's verdict refuses to declare either technique the safer bet. WHY-NOT-C (trap: role_or_attribution_swap — the TYPE-005 signature): this is Marek's quoted position — 'A shape is a decision made once' — offered as the writer's. The text frames it as put 'without qualification' and answers it immediately with Rask's correction. WHY-NOT-D (trap: polarity overshoot): dismissiveness overshoots a verdict that grants shaping a genuine, non-decaying advantage; nothing in the passage calls the preference vanity, and 'entirely discredited' is contradicted by the concession that shaped towers 'do not drift'.

generator_meta.topic: how tall buildings manage wind: tuned mass dampers versus aerodynamic shaping
